title: Extreme Heat Poses Greater Danger to Older Adults Than Previously Understood
excerpt: New research shows heat-related mortality among people over 65 has surged by 85% since the early 2000s, with India's elderly population among the most vulnerable globally.
body:
• Heat-related mortality among adults over 65 has risen approximately 85% since the early 2000s, driven by aging populations moving into hotter regions.
  • By 2050, nearly a quarter of the world's older adults — 246 million more people — could face dangerous temperature extremes above 37.5°C, with India, Pakistan and China most affected.
  • India lost an estimated 247 billion labor hours to heat exposure in 2024 alone, with the elderly, outdoor workers and those with chronic conditions bearing the greatest burden.

Extreme heat is killing and hospitalizing older adults at rates far higher than scientists previously estimated, according to a convergence of recent research that paints an alarming picture for aging populations worldwide — and for India in particular.

A comprehensive review published in The Lancet's eBioMedicine found that heat-related mortality among people over 65 increased by roughly 85% between the first five years of the 21st century and the 2017–2021 period. A separate meta-analysis cited in the review estimated that all-cause mortality rises by 2% to 5% for each 1°C increase in ambient temperature above regional thresholds during hot weather.

A Perfect Storm of Aging and Warming

A study published in Nature Communications projects that by 2050, an additional 246 million adults aged 69 and older could face temperatures exceeding 37.5°C — meaning more than 23% of the global older population would be exposed to dangerous heat levels, up from 14% today.

"It's this kind of perfect storm of biological aging, social loneliness and then cognition that make heat so much worse for older people."

— Deborah Carr, sociologist of aging, Boston University

The biological mechanics are well documented. Aging bodies lose thermoregulatory efficiency. Chronic conditions like cardiovascular disease and diabetes — common in older populations — worsen under heat stress. Medications for blood pressure, depression and other conditions can be dehydrating or interfere with sweating. And social isolation, limited mobility and cognitive decline leave many elderly people unable to take protective measures even when warnings are issued.

India at the Frontlines

India faces a particularly acute version of this crisis. The 2025 Lancet Countdown found that climate change drove nearly one-third of the country's heatwave days in 2024. Heat exposure cost India an estimated 247 billion potential labor hours last year, primarily in agriculture and construction — an economic loss of roughly $194 billion, according to the report.

Research from the University of Toronto and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine found that Indian adults over 65 are 2.5 times more likely to die during extreme temperature events. With India's elderly population projected to grow rapidly in the coming decades, the intersection of demographic aging and climate warming presents a public health challenge of enormous scale.

The UNEP's Frontiers 2025 Report, released as heatwaves gripped communities across India, China, Europe and the United States, warned that annual heat-related deaths among older persons have risen by an estimated 85% since the 1990s globally. The report specifically flagged low- and middle-income countries — where older populations are growing fastest and cooling infrastructure is least available — as high-risk zones.

Beyond Individual Risk

The threat extends beyond mortality statistics. A Reuters analysis of heat health risks noted that globally, just under half a million deaths per year are attributed to excess heat, though data from many low-income countries remains incomplete. A European study found climate change was responsible for 68% of the estimated 24,400 heat deaths in 854 European cities in 2025.

"Heat waves are a silent and invisible killer. We don't often see the impact that they have had on human health until the mortality statistics are published many months later."

— Liz Stephens, Professor of Climate Risk and Resilience, University of Reading

What Needs to Change

Researchers and public health experts are calling for targeted interventions: early warning systems calibrated for elderly populations, heat action plans in municipalities with aging demographics, and infrastructure investments in cooling centers and green urban spaces.

For India's diaspora communities, the implications are personal. Many have aging parents in regions where summer temperatures routinely exceed safe thresholds, and where access to air conditioning and healthcare remains uneven. The research makes clear that protecting older populations from extreme heat is no longer a future concern — it is a present emergency that will only intensify as both temperatures and the average age of the population continue to climb.
